title: He learned obedience (Hebrews 5:7–10)
hookLine: with loud cries and tears, he learned through what he suffered
tomorrow: what holds a boat that's still rocking?

lines: THE WORST YEAR, THE MOST LEARNED?
cards: Some people say the worst year of their life taught them the most. Others say that's a story told to make pain sound useful. Can suffering teach anything?

Hebrews gives a glimpse of Jesus praying, and it isn't serene: "Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared."

teach.b: Then a line some readers find startling: "Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered." Though he were a Son: the writer knows how strange that sounds.
It isn't fixing a fault; the chapter before has just said he was without sin. It's learning the way feet learn a road by walking it: obedience known from the inside, at a cost.

teach.h: HEARD, AND STILL THE ROAD WENT THROUGH.
teach.b: And notice: he was heard, and still the road went all the way through. Then: "And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him."
Perfect here reads less like polished and more like complete, brought all the way. So that's Hebrews' answer.
Suffering isn't called good in itself, but it can be a road someone learns on, and Christians say he walked it first. A neighbor tradition sits close by.

teach.h: THE QUR'AN: WITH HARDSHIP GOETH EASE.
teach.b: The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, comforts: "with hardship goeth ease." And it says, "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope."
Shared ground: hardship isn't the end of the story, and the one who suffers isn't left alone in it.
One honest difference: Hebrews says the one who cried and learned was the Son.
Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet and messenger of God, not as God's Son, and in the Qur'an the comfort comes from God to the one in hardship. Two traditions, each in its own words.

how: Some Christians read Hebrews 5:7–9 in Holy Week, beside the Gospel accounts of Jesus praying before his arrest.

games.q: a friend's dad lost his job, and someone tells her, 'God's teaching him a lesson.' she's furious. what's closer to Hebrews 5?
o: suffering can be a road someone learns on, without being a punishment.
every hardship is a punishment for something done wrong.
real faith means hardship teaches nothing and should be ignored.
games.why: Hebrews says the Son, without sin, learned obedience by what he suffered: learning on a hard road, not a punishment.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one line about a hard season that's behind you, not the hardest, just one, and what it taught you that nothing easy could have.
Then set the pen down for the rest of the sit, and let the line be true rather than tidy. If no hard season feels ready to write about yet, a small one will do.

wordCard.voice: He learned obedience. Hebrews five: a Son who prayed with strong crying and tears, was heard, and learned obedience by what he suffered.

orig.note: Greek: he learned; in Hebrews 5:8 it sits beside epathen, he suffered.

carryVoice: The line to keep: learned through suffering, and heard all the way through. Go gently.
